world_behind.title: The money table is the setup for the bribe
world_behind.text: Sixteen verses on weights and measures look like an interruption. They are the reason verse 22 lands: when Zeezrom offers "six onties of silver" (v. 22), the reader has just been taught that an onti "was as great as them all" (v. 13). Without the table the offer is a number. With it, the reader knows a judge earned one senum a day and can do the arithmetic on what six of the largest silver measure would buy.

cites.quote: was as great as them all

spans.text: was as great as them all

world_behind.title: Judges were paid by the day
world_behind.text: The law of Mosiah set the rate at "a senine of gold for a day" (v. 3) for time actually spent judging. Pay tied to caseload is a system with an appetite, and verse 20 says what these men did with it.

cites.quote: a senine of gold for a day

spans.text: a senine of gold for a day

world_behind.title: The Nephites had left the Jewish system behind
world_behind.text: Verse 4 says outright that they "altered their reckoning" (v. 4) and did not measure after the manner of the Jews at Jerusalem. The record pauses to explain its own units because it knows a reader will not have them. The same instinct made it explain what a lawyer was one chapter earlier.

world_behind.title: Grain is the anchor of the whole scale
world_behind.text: A senum of silver buys a measure of barley (v. 7), and a shiblon buys half a measure (v. 15). The system is pinned to food rather than to metal, so every figure in the chapter can be read as days of eating.

world_behind.title: This is a courtroom scene in a city with no court in session
world_behind.text: The vocabulary is legal throughout: wages, evidences, officers, compelled to pay, questions put and answered, lying before God, and at the end a bar to be arraigned at. Zeezrom questions Amulek the way he would question a defendant, and Amulek answers in the same genre.

world_behind.title: The catechism has a shape
world_behind.text: Zeezrom's questions move from the existence of God, to the number of Gods, to how Amulek knows, to who is coming, to whether he will save people in their sins. It is a ladder, and verse 35 shows what it was built for: a summary he can read back to the crowd.

world_behind.title: Bribery of a judge was an old offense
world_behind.text: Samuel's sons turned aside after lucre and perverted judgment, and that ended the era of judges in Israel. Alma 11 is set inside a system of judges that began four books earlier, and the same word for corrupt money appears at its unravelling.

words.text: Counting, and the system used to count. Four of the five times this record uses the noun fall in this chapter, and the fifth is about keeping time. Here it means the whole conversion table: what a coin is worth against another coin, and both against barley. The record tells the reader that the Nephites built their own, a small declaration of independence buried in an accounting note.

The largest silver measure, "as great as them all" (v. 13). The word appears twice in the reckoning table and then, in its plural, in Zeezrom's hand. A reader who skipped verses 5 through 19 cannot feel verse 22. The chapter teaches the denomination and then spends it, and the offer is the top of the scale multiplied by six.

Money, with the taint already in the word. The King James Bible keeps it for corrupt office holders: bishops who must not be greedy of filthy lucre, and Samuel's sons, who were judges and "turned aside after lucre" and perverted judgment. Amulek uses it on a man whose income depends on the volume of lawsuits, and the choice of word puts him in that lineage.

Bonds, what ties a prisoner. Death is not described as a place or a sleep in this passage; it is a restraint, and what Christ does to it is "the loosing of the bands of death" (v. 41). The image makes resurrection an act of release performed on everyone, which is exactly the claim of verse 44: it comes to the wicked as surely as the righteous.

cites.quote: the loosing of the bands of death

spans.text: the loosing of the bands of death

words.text: The act of calling something back to mind. The word occurs once in all of scripture, here, in the phrase "a bright recollection of all our guilt" (v. 43). Bright is doing the work. What the resurrection restores is not only limb and joint but clarity, and the passage treats undimmed memory as part of what makes standing there difficult.

cites.quote: a bright recollection of all our guilt

spans.text: a bright recollection of all our guilt

words.text: To be brought before a court and formally charged. Another word used once in the whole of scripture, and it arrives at the end of the most legal chapter in the book, spoken to a lawyer who has spent the afternoon trying to catch a man in his words. The scene Zeezrom controls is being described to him with his own vocabulary, relocated.

phrases.term: A senine of gold for a day
phrases.text: The wage that sets the scale. Everything else in the chapter's arithmetic can be measured against a day of a judge's time, itself a measure of barley. The record gives the number without comment and lets it do its work nineteen verses later.

Six hundred years from Jerusalem, and the measures have drifted. The record says so plainly and then supplies the table, treating its own distance from the old world as an ordinary fact needing an ordinary footnote.

phrases.term: That they might have more employ
phrases.text: The mechanism of the corruption in five words. The lawyers did not take bribes to lose cases. They manufactured disorder so there would be more cases, since the pay followed the work. The record describes an incentive rather than a conspiracy.

The price offered for a denial of God, stated in the largest unit on the table. The offer is generous by the chapter's own arithmetic, and Amulek's answer treats the generosity as beside the point. Verse 25 then says the money was never going to be paid.

phrases.term: Thou lovest that lucre more than him
phrases.text: Amulek's diagnosis, and it does not accuse Zeezrom of unbelief. It accuses him of ranking. The sentence grants that the man knows there is a God and locates the problem in what he prefers, which is a harder charge and a more common one.

phrases.term: Thou hadst it in thy heart to retain them from me
phrases.text: The bribe was a trap and the money was never leaving his hand. Amulek names the intent, and the accusation names God as the one lied to. A lawyer setting a perjury trap is caught in one.

phrases.term: Shall he save his people in their sins
phrases.text: The question the whole exchange was built to reach. Answer yes and the Son is indulgent; answer no and it sounds like a limit on God. That is how Zeezrom immediately reports it to the crowd. Amulek takes the second horn and explains it by the nature of God's word.

phrases.term: It is impossible for him to deny his word
phrases.text: The reason underneath the answer. What constrains God here is not weakness or reluctance; it is consistency. The record will build a good deal on this later, and it enters at the point where a hostile lawyer asked a question sharp enough to require it.

phrases.term: No unclean thing can inherit the kingdom of heaven
phrases.text: The premise Amulek supplies to close the argument. Salvation in sins would mean an unclean thing inheriting, which the word of God has already ruled out. The logic is short and it converts a debating point into a definition.

phrases.term: The very Eternal Father of heaven and of earth
phrases.text: Zeezrom's question was probably meant to expose a contradiction, and the answer he gets is more, not less, than he asked for: beginning and end, first and last. Whatever trap was set, the reply refuses to narrow.

phrases.term: A bright recollection of all our guilt
phrases.text: The most uncomfortable clause in the resurrection passage. Bodies come back whole and so does memory, undimmed. Judgment in this account requires no evidence brought against a person, since the person will remember.

phrases.term: Not so much as a hair of their heads be lost
phrases.text: Physical specificity taken to its limit, and applied to everyone. The verse lists old and young, bond and free, male and female, wicked and righteous, and then refuses to let even a hair go missing from any of them. The completeness is the doctrine.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: The law on wages
verses.text: Judges are paid by the day for time spent judging, with the rate fixed by the law of Mosiah. Two verses of civil procedure, including how a debtor is brought in and compelled to pay, and then the number.

verses.label: v. 4–19
verses.title: The reckoning
verses.text: Gold in four denominations, silver in four, then the lesser numbers, all pinned to measures of barley. The record explains that the Nephites built their own system. Nothing in these verses is doctrine and none of it is wasted.

verses.label: v. 20–21
verses.title: The motive, and the man
verses.text: One verse names what the lawyers were doing and why, and the next introduces Zeezrom asking politely whether Amulek will answer a few questions. The politeness is reported alongside the description of him as expert in the devices of the devil.

verses.label: v. 22–25
verses.title: The offer, and the refusal
verses.text: Six onties for a denial. Amulek declines, then goes further and tells Zeezrom what was actually in his heart: the money was bait and would have stayed in his hand. The exchange takes four verses and ends the bribery attempt for good.

verses.label: v. 26–37
verses.title: The examination
verses.text: Short questions, short answers, moving from one God to the coming Son to whether he saves people in their sins. Zeezrom turns to the crowd in verse 35 with his summary, and Amulek spends two verses taking it apart.

verses.label: v. 38–41
verses.title: The answer that opens out
verses.text: Asked whether the Son is the Eternal Father, Amulek says yes and keeps going: heaven and earth, beginning and end, first and last, redemption for those who believe, and the loosing of death's bands for everyone.

verses.label: v. 42–46
verses.title: The resurrection, and a man trembling
verses.text: Temporal death undone, spirit and body reunited in perfect form, limb and joint restored, memory bright, all classes of people included, everyone arraigned. Then the crowd is astonished again and Zeezrom begins to shake.

chapter.title: The accounting is the argument
chapter.text: A modern reader skims verses 4 through 19 as a table. Placed where they are, they set the price of the offer that follows, and the chapter's structure says that a man with a scale in his head can recognize what he is being offered. The record teaches the reader to value the bribe before showing it.

chapter.title: A lawyer is answered in law
chapter.text: Zeezrom's method is cross-examination, and Amulek does not object to the form. He answers the questions, then charges Zeezrom with lying before God and gives the evidence of intent. The chapter ends with a courtroom image nobody in it controls.

chapter.title: The corruption is structural
chapter.text: Verse 20 puts the fault in the pay structure. Pay by the case and cases will multiply. The record diagnoses a system. That is why the chapter opens with the wage law.

chapter.title: Doctrine arrives because someone hostile asked for it
chapter.text: The fullest statement on resurrection so far in the record is produced under cross-examination by a man trying to destroy the witness. The book gets its clearest teaching out of its worst room.

chapter.title: Salvation is bounded by consistency
chapter.text: Amulek's ground for saying the Son cannot save people in their sins is that he cannot deny his word. That places the limit inside God's own character, and the record will return to it whenever mercy and justice are argued.

chapter.title: The resurrection is described physically and universally
chapter.text: Limb, joint, frame, hair. Old and young, bond and free, male and female, wicked and righteous. Nothing in the passage is offered as comfort and nothing is withheld from anyone.

chapter.title: Memory is part of judgment
chapter.text: Bright recollection of guilt does work that no external accusation could. It makes the judgment scene quiet, and it removes any question of the record being wrong.

chapter.title: The chapter ends with a symptom
chapter.text: Zeezrom trembles. He has not repented, argued back, or conceded anything, and the record notes only the shaking. What that turns into occupies the next three chapters.

applications.title: Know the exchange rate before the offer comes
applications.text: The chapter arms its reader with the table first. Work out in advance what your integrity is priced at in the currencies you actually deal in: time, standing, a job, a relationship. The offer is easier to see when you already know the scale.

applications.title: Look for the incentive first
applications.text: The lawyers stirred up trouble because trouble paid. Before assuming bad character in a situation that keeps going wrong, ask what the arrangement rewards, and whether anyone would have to be wicked for it to produce this.

applications.title: Answer the question and then name the move
applications.text: Amulek did not refuse to engage, and he did not pretend the exchange was innocent. He did both: gave the answer, then said what was being attempted. Most people manage only one.

applications.title: Assume the record of your own life is complete
applications.text: The passage puts nothing in the hands of witnesses. Take one thing you have been hoping is filed somewhere out of reach, and deal with it as though you will one day remember it clearly.

questions.text: What am I paid by, and what does that arrangement quietly encourage me to produce more of?
Where have I benefited from a problem I also helped keep alive?
What is the largest offer I have ever received to be quiet about something true, and what did I do?
Which do I actually prefer when they conflict, and would someone watching my week be able to tell?
Do I want to be saved from my sins or in them, and which am I praying for?
What would a bright recollection of my own guilt include that I have already talked myself out of?
When did I last tremble at something true, and what did I do with the next hour?
